lesson.title: When the Plains Turned to Dust
lesson.summary: In the 1930s, years of drought combined with farming practices that had stripped away the prairie's protective grasses turned millions of acres of the southern Great Plains into a landscape of choking dust storms, deepening the misery of the Great Depression for farm families across the region.
lesson.body:
During and after World War I, wheat prices were high, and farmers across the southern Great Plains, in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado, and New Mexico, plowed up vast stretches of native grassland to plant wheat and other cash crops. Those grasses had deep, tangled root systems that had held the region's thin topsoil in place through centuries of drought. Removing them, combined with the overproduction and heavy debt loads that were already straining the farm economy and helping set up the broader causes of the Great Depression, left the soil with nothing to anchor it once the rains stopped.

The drought arrived in the early 1930s and did not let up for years, with the worst conditions concentrated between 1934 and 1936. Without grass roots or moisture to hold it together, the exposed topsoil turned to fine dust that the plains winds lifted into enormous, rolling clouds called black blizzards. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, DC, and out over the Atlantic Ocean. The single worst storm, remembered as Black Sunday, struck on April 14, 1935, turning day into darkness across the region in minutes. Farm families breathed grit that caused a respiratory illness known as dust pneumonia, lost livestock and crops, and watched topsoil that had taken centuries to form blow away in an afternoon.

The crisis was not simply bad luck with weather. It was the predictable result of farming methods that treated the grassland as an inexhaustible resource rather than a fragile system. That lesson pushed the federal government to act: soil scientist Hugh Hammond Bennett testified before Congress in 1935 while a dust storm from the plains was visibly darkening the skies over the capital, helping win passage of the Soil Conservation Act and the creation of the Soil Conservation Service. New Deal programs paid farmers to practice contour plowing, crop rotation, and terracing, and to plant rows of trees called shelterbelts to break the wind.

For many tenant farmers and sharecroppers, the same economic pressures that had already made farm labor precarious, low crop prices, mounting debt, and landlords eager to consolidate land, meant that a few failed harvests were enough to wipe them out entirely. Banks foreclosed on farms across the region, leaving families with little choice but to pack what they could carry and leave. That mass departure from the Dust Bowl states set the stage for one of the largest internal migrations in American history.
